scenario.title: Support backlog
scenario.initial_request: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

M-TICKET-RESPONSE-TIME.name: Median ticket response time versus SLA

M-REFUND-FAILURE-COUNT.name: Count of refund payments failed due to invalid IBAN format

M-IBAN-FAILURE-RATE.name: Rate of refund payments failing due to invalid IBAN format
M-IBAN-FAILURE-RATE.numerator: refund payment records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (payment-db)
M-IBAN-FAILURE-RATE.denominator: total refund payment attempts recorded in payment-db

M-REFUND-STATUS-TICKET-VOLUME.name: Volume of tickets inquiring about refund status
M-REFUND-STATUS-TICKET-VOLUME.population: tickets tagged as refund-status inquiries in ticket-db

F-01.statement: ticket-db reports a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets.

F-02.statement: payment-db.refund_failures reports 5 refund records, all with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT.

CL-01.statement: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

CL-02.statement: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

H-SLOW-RESPONSE.statement: The root cause is that customers wait too long to receive an answer to refund-status questions, and automating answers (chatbot) would resolve it.

H-PROCESS-DELAY.statement: The root cause is actual delay in the refund process itself (P-REF) — payments taking long to complete — so tickets accumulate because the underlying refund hasn't happened, not because answers are slow.

H-TICKET-VOLUME-SURGE.statement: The root cause is a high volume of repetitive status-check tickets caused by lack of self-service visibility into refund status, not slowness of any individual response.

H-SUPPORT-CAPACITY.statement: The root cause is overall support team capacity/staffing shortfall causing backlog across ticket types, with refunds being only one visible symptom.

H-IBAN-FAILURE.statement: Refunds fail to complete because of invalid IBAN format data (payment-db shows FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), and these unresolved failed payments generate the refund-status tickets, rather than slow responses or capacity.

interpretation_history.interpretation: Ticket-db shows a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets — responses are generally fast, not slow, which undermines the premise that customers wait too long for answers.

payment-db shows 5 refund records failed with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, i.e. the refund payments themselves did not complete due to a data/validation error, independent of support response speed. This points to a refund-processing failure mechanism (not merely slowness) as a plausible driver of the ticket backlog.

E-03.content: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-SUP (the same stakeholder behind CL-01) reiterates the view that customers wait too long for refund answers and that a chatbot would fix it; this is a restatement of the existing claim, not new evidence, and does not address the response-time data (E-01) or payment failures (E-02) already on record.

U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE.question: What proportion of the refund-status ticket backlog is attributable to IBAN-format refund failures versus other mechanisms (e.g. self-service visibility gaps or genuine processing delay)?
U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE.decision_impact: Determines whether fixing IBAN failures alone resolves the backlog or whether additional remediation (self-service status visibility, process-delay fixes) is also needed.
U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE.resolution_path: Join ticket-db refund-status tickets to payment-db failed-refund records by refund/customer id and compute the coverage percentage.
U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE.safe_placeholder: Proceed with correcting the 5 known IBAN-format failures without building broader self-service/chatbot features until coverage is confirmed.

U-FAILURE-RESOLUTION-MECHANISM.question: Do FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds get retried or corrected automatically, or do they require manual stakeholder/customer action to fix the IBAN data?
U-FAILURE-RESOLUTION-MECHANISM.decision_impact: Determines whether the solution needs an automated reprocessing step or a manual data-correction workflow, and who must be notified.
U-FAILURE-RESOLUTION-MECHANISM.resolution_path: Inspect the payment-db refund workflow/IBAN validation logic for existing retry policy.
U-FAILURE-RESOLUTION-MECHANISM.safe_placeholder: Manually review and correct the 5 failed records before building any automated reprocessing.

U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE.question: Does the 2.0h median response time (E-01, 900 tickets) specifically cover refund-status tickets, or is it an aggregate across all ticket types?
U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE.decision_impact: If refund-status tickets are not well represented in the 900-ticket sample, the conclusion that responses are 'fast' may not hold for the ticket category the problem is about, affecting confidence in rejecting the slow-response hypothesis.
U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE.resolution_path: Filter ticket-db response_times by refund-status category and recompute the median.
U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE.safe_placeholder: Treat the fast-response finding as directional only; do not use it alone to rule out a slow-response issue specific to refund tickets.

U-COMPETING-MECHANISMS.question: Is the backlog also driven by lack of self-service refund-status visibility (H-TICKET-VOLUME-SURGE) or genuine refund-process delay (H-PROCESS-DELAY), independent of or in addition to IBAN failures?
U-COMPETING-MECHANISMS.decision_impact: Would expand or redirect solution scope beyond IBAN-format correction if either candidate mechanism turns out to be a significant contributor.
U-COMPETING-MECHANISMS.resolution_path: Categorize ticket-db refund tickets by sub-reason and correlate with payment-db status/delay data to quantify each candidate mechanism's share.
U-COMPETING-MECHANISMS.safe_placeholder: Limit solution scope to the confirmed IBAN-format correction until the other candidate mechanisms are quantified.

A-FAILURE-TICKET-LINKAGE.statement: The 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refund records (E-02) are assumed to drive refund-status tickets in ticket-db, though no record directly links specific tickets to specific failed refunds.

A-BACKLOG-COVERAGE.statement: IBAN-format refund failures are assumed to be a materially contributing share of the refund-status ticket backlog rather than an isolated edge case, given 5 failures against a 900-ticket base.

SC-ZERO-FAILED-REFUNDS.statement: All refund payments currently in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status (5 records, E-02) are corrected and successfully processed.
SC-ZERO-FAILED-REFUNDS.validation_method: Query payment-db.refund_failures and confirm the count of FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status records is zero.

SC-REDUCED-REFUND-TICKETS.statement: Refund-status ticket volume decreases after the failed refunds are resolved, indicating the fix addresses a real driver of the ticket backlog.
SC-REDUCED-REFUND-TICKETS.threshold: measurable decrease comparing a baseline period to a post-fix period
SC-REDUCED-REFUND-TICKETS.validation_method: Compare ticket-db refund-status ticket counts for a defined period before and after refund correction.

VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE.unresolved_question: What proportion of the refund-status ticket backlog is attributable to IBAN-format refund failures versus other mechanisms (e.g. self-service visibility gaps or genuine processing delay)?
VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE.reason_deferred: deferred at DEFINE Gate; safe placeholder: Proceed with correcting the 5 known IBAN-format failures without building broader self-service/chatbot features until coverage is confirmed.
VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE.validation_method: Join ticket-db refund-status tickets to payment-db failed-refund records by refund/customer id and compute the coverage percentage.

VOB-U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE.unresolved_question: Does the 2.0h median response time (E-01, 900 tickets) specifically cover refund-status tickets, or is it an aggregate across all ticket types?
VOB-U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE.reason_deferred: deferred at DEFINE Gate; safe placeholder: Treat the fast-response finding as directional only; do not use it alone to rule out a slow-response issue specific to refund tickets.
VOB-U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE.validation_method: Filter ticket-db response_times by refund-status category and recompute the median.

VOB-R-3.unresolved_question: Do FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds get retried or corrected automatically, or do they require manual stakeholder/customer action to fix the IBAN data?
VOB-R-3.reason_deferred: proposed by reasoner R-10: U-FAILURE-RESOLUTION-MECHANISM is OPEN and affects_scope includes reprocess_refund_payment:DA-PAY, so executing the write without knowing the mechanism risks an incorrect protected action.
VOB-R-3.validation_method: Check documented refund-processing procedure or ask the payment-ops stakeholder whether reprocessing after an IBAN correction is automatic.
required_evidence: Stakeholder confirmation of manual vs automatic resolution step

VOB-R-4.unresolved_question: Is the ticket backlog also driven by lack of self-service refund-status visibility or genuine refund-process delay, independent of or in addition to IBAN failures?
VOB-R-4.reason_deferred: proposed by reasoner R-10: U-COMPETING-MECHANISMS is OPEN and affects_scope includes monitor_refund_failure_rate:DA-TCK, so the monitoring signal's meaning for SC-REDUCED-REFUND-TICKETS is unverified.
VOB-R-4.validation_method: Analyze ticket-db for competing backlog drivers (self-service visibility gaps, process delay) alongside IBAN-failure correlation.
required_evidence: Confirmation of whether self-service status visibility exists

problem_definition.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers get instant answers to refund-status questions instead of waiting (CL-01, the stakeholder's initial request).
symptoms: Support lead reports customers waiting for refund-status answers and requests a chatbot to answer instantly (CL-01, CL-02/E-03).
payment-db shows 5 refund payment records failed with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-02).
ticket-db shows a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets, i.e. responses are generally fast, not slow (E-01).
problem_definition.root_problem: Refund-status tickets accumulate not because support responses are slow (E-01: median 2.0h vs a 24h SLA across 900 tickets) but because a subset of refund payments fail at the payment-processing step due to invalid IBAN format (E-02: 5 records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), leaving those refunds unresolved and prompting customers to open or escalate tickets about them.

structural_remedies.description: Correct invalid IBAN data on the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records in payment-db (correct_iban_format_data on DA-PAY).
structural_remedies.rationale: Only 5 records so fast, but payment-db is read_only in tool_surface and domain_authorizations is empty, so no write authority exists yet.; residual gap: Does not by itself confirm this reduces ticket volume; U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE remains open.

structural_remedies.description: Reprocess the corrected refunds (reprocess_refund_payment on DA-PAY) so they complete, satisfying SC-ZERO-FAILED-REFUNDS.
structural_remedies.rationale: Small bounded action but requires write access to payment-db not granted by current read-only tool_surface/empty domain_authorizations.; residual gap: U-FAILURE-RESOLUTION-MECHANISM is open: unclear if retry is automatic or needs manual/customer action.

structural_remedies.description: Notify affected customers (notify_affected_customers on DA-TCK) once refunds are corrected, to close/forestall related tickets.
structural_remedies.rationale: Low volume and simple, but ticket-db is also read_only in tool_surface with no write/notify authorization present.; residual gap: Depends on prior correction/reprocessing; does not address other possible backlog mechanisms (U-COMPETING-MECHANISMS).

structural_remedies.description: Monitor M-IBAN-FAILURE-RATE and refund-status ticket volume (monitor_refund_failure_rate on DA-PAY/DA-TCK) via existing read-only queries.
structural_remedies.rationale: Pure read-only querying matches current tool_surface and needs no new authorizations.; residual gap: Detects recurrence but does not fix the 5 existing failures or resolve open attribution/metric-scope unknowns.

structural_remedies.description: Add IBAN validation at refund intake (process/config change to P-REF) to prevent future format failures.
structural_remedies.rationale: P-REF has no documented steps/systems; changing intake logic is outside the current read-only tool_surface and listed scope actions, so cannot be designed/executed now.; residual gap: Even if built later, leaves the existing 5 failed refunds and open backlog-attribution unknowns unresolved.

decision_log.rationale: causal chain: Customer submits a refund request that is routed for payment processing (P-REF). → The refund payment attempt fails validation due to invalid IBAN format, recorded in payment-db as FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-02). → The failed refund payment remains unresolved, so the customer's refund never actually completes. → The customer opens or follows up on a support ticket asking about refund status, contributing to the ticket backlog even though the median response time is a fast 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA (E-01).; rejected framings: [('H-SLOW-RESPONSE', 'Contradicted by E-01 (median 2.0h response against a 24h SLA across 900 tickets, i.e. fast not slow) and by E-02 (the real issue is a payment-processing failure, not response speed); status REJECTED.'), ('H-SUPPORT-CAPACITY', 'Contradicted by E-01, which shows generally fast response times with no supporting evidence of a staffing/capacity shortfall; status REJECTED and has no supporting evidence.')]

[CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE deferred to VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE; [CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE deferred to VOB-U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE

framing_assertion.rationale: The initial request (B-CHATBOT) asserts that customers 'waiting for answers about refunds' is solved by faster answering (a chatbot), framing the problem as response latency per SH-SUP.

hypotheses.statement: The root cause is that customers wait too long to receive an answer to refund-status questions, and automating answers (chatbot) would resolve it.
hypotheses.rationale: This is SH-SUP's stated framing of the problem, but SH-SUP has a noted potential_bias of 'frames everything as response speed', so it must be tested rather than adopted.
discriminating_evidence: ticket-db response times for refund-tagged tickets
correlation between ticket response time and ticket close/resolution outcome

hypotheses.statement: The root cause is actual delay in the refund process itself (P-REF) — payments taking long to complete — so tickets accumulate because the underlying refund hasn't happened, not because answers are slow.
hypotheses.rationale: If true, a chatbot would only mask the symptom by answering faster while the actual refund (DA-PAY) is still stuck, requiring a process fix in P-REF rather than a communication tool.
discriminating_evidence: payment-db refund processing/completion timestamps vs. ticket creation timestamps
proportion of refund tickets opened while payment status is still pending in DA-PAY

hypotheses.statement: The root cause is a high volume of repetitive status-check tickets caused by lack of self-service visibility into refund status, not slowness of any individual response.
hypotheses.rationale: If customers mainly lack a way to check status themselves, a self-service status page could resolve the backlog with less effort than a full chatbot, changing the solution shape.
discriminating_evidence: ticket-db ticket reason/category breakdown for refund tickets
repeat-contact rate per refund case in ticket-db

hypotheses.statement: The root cause is overall support team capacity/staffing shortfall causing backlog across ticket types, with refunds being only one visible symptom.
hypotheses.rationale: If the backlog is a general capacity issue rather than refund-specific, the fix would be staffing/triage changes rather than a refund-focused chatbot.
discriminating_evidence: ticket-db response times across non-refund ticket categories
backlog volume trend over time in ticket-db

actions.question: What are current refund-ticket response times and how do volumes break down by ticket type/reason?
actions.expected_information_gain: Reveals whether response times are actually slow and whether backlog is driven by repetitive status checks or broader capacity strain, directly testing H-SLOW-RESPONSE, H-TICKET-VOLUME-SURGE and H-SUPPORT-CAPACITY.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: Determines whether a chatbot (answer-speed fix) is even aimed at the real bottleneck versus volume or staffing issues.
actions.why_now: CL-01 is an unverified stakeholder framing (SH-SUP has known bias toward response-speed framing per DA-TCK/ticket-db); this read-only query can test it cheaply before committing to a chatbot solution.

actions.question: Are refund payments themselves experiencing delays or failures in process P-REF, independent of ticket response times?
actions.expected_information_gain: Confirms or rules out H-PROCESS-DELAY: if refunds themselves are slow/failing, a chatbot would mask rather than fix the problem.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: If actual refund processing is delayed, building a chatbot would be the wrong intervention entirely, redirecting the whole project.
actions.why_now: DA-PAY data is authoritative but completeness is UNKNOWN; checking it now is low-cost and critical before any solution choice.

actions.question: Beyond response speed, does the support team see capacity/staffing strain or ticket-type patterns suggesting other causes of the refund backlog?
actions.expected_information_gain: May surface additional context on staffing or ticket mix, but SH-SUP's known bias ('frames everything as response speed') limits new discriminative value versus the tool-query evidence.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: Low marginal value since CL-01 already captures this stakeholder's framing and bias is already documented.
actions.why_now: Could still corroborate or add nuance to CL-01 but is lower priority than the two direct data queries.

proposal.stop_reason: Two unexecuted read-only tool queries (ticket-db response_times, payment-db refund_failures) can still directly test competing root-cause hypotheses before any solution decision, so discovery is not exhausted.

proposal.interpretation: Ticket-db shows a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets — responses are generally fast, not slow, which undermines the premise that customers wait too long for answers.

hypothesis_effects.rationale: Median response time (2.0h) is far below the 24h SLA across 900 tickets, inconsistent with a root cause of slow answers to refund questions.
A fast median response across 900 tickets argues against a general staffing/capacity backlog causing delayed handling.
Response-time data confirms ticket count (900) but says nothing about whether tickets are repetitive status checks caused by lack of self-service visibility.
This metric concerns ticket response speed, not the refund payment process itself, so it neither confirms nor refutes delay in P-REF.

contradiction_assessment.rationale: No explicit problem_definition is present in state to assess this observation against.

vob_proposals.validation_method: Run payment-db:refund_failures to check for actual processing delays in P-REF and examine ticket content for repetitive status-check patterns.
vob_proposals.rationale: The chatbot's stated justification (slow response) is contradicted by fast median response times, so the true driver of the backlog must be confirmed before committing to a chatbot solution.

proposal.summary: The support lead's initial request (CL-01) was to build a chatbot because customers 'wait forever' for refund-status answers (CL-01, CL-02, E-03). Evidence contradicted that framing: ticket-db shows a median response time of 2.0h against a 24h SLA across 900 tickets (E-01), so responses are generally fast, not slow (hypothesis H-SLOW-RESPONSE rejected). Instead, payment-db shows 5 refund records stuck in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status (E-02), supporting the hypothesis (H-IBAN-FAILURE) that unresolved failed refunds, not slow replies, are driving refund-status tickets. The problem was redefined accordingly in PD-1, which passed the DEFINE gate as CONDITIONAL_PASS with two critical unknowns deferred as VOBs. The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION (no holds): the planned remediation (correct the IBAN data and reprocess the 5 failed refunds on DA-PAY, then notify affected customers via DA-TCK) is released, while monitoring (monitor_refund_failure_rate) is withheld because it is blocked by open critical VOBs on both data targets. Several open questions remain unresolved but are judged outside the release's blocking scope, so the release proceeds with those limitations documented rather than held.
key_points: Root problem per PD-1: refund-status tickets accumulate because 5 refund payments failed with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-02), leaving refunds unresolved, not because support responses are slow (E-01 shows 2.0h median vs 24h SLA across 900 tickets).

The original chatbot request (CL-01/CL-02, from SH-SUP, who the data flags as biased toward framing issues as response speed) was tested against evidence and the slow-response hypothesis (H-SLOW-RESPONSE) was rejected using E-01 and E-02.

DEFINE gate result was CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two HIGH-criticality unknowns (U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE and U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE) as VOBs, both judged outside the release's blocking scope.

Release scope (SD-1): correct_iban_format_data on DA-PAY, reprocess_refund_payment on DA-PAY, and notify_affected_customers on DA-TCK; monitor_refund_failure_rate was withheld because both its targets (DA-PAY, DA-TCK) are blocked by open critical VOBs.

Decision: RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION with no holds; VOB-R-3 (whether failed-refund correction is automatic or needs manual action) intersects release scope but was treated as non-critical, while VOB-R-4 and VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE/VOB-U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE remain open outside scope.

Success criteria for the released fix are SC-ZERO-FAILED-REFUNDS (0 remaining FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records in payment-db) and SC-REDUCED-REFUND-TICKETS (measurable drop in refund-status ticket volume post-fix).
Preventive process work (adding IBAN validation at refund intake, P-REF) and the monitoring action were left unfinished/out of this release.
limitations_explained: The 2.0h median response time (E-01) was computed across all 900 tickets and is not confirmed to isolate refund-status inquiries specifically, so it may not fully represent the refund-ticket experience.
A-FAILURE-TICKET-LINKAGE is an unverified assumption: no record directly ties the 5 failed refunds (E-02) to specific tickets, so the notify_affected_customers action may mis-target customers.
It is unknown (U-FAILURE-RESOLUTION-MECHANISM / VOB-R-3) whether FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds can be reprocessed automatically or require manual stakeholder/customer action to correct the IBAN data.

monitor_refund_failure_rate was excluded from the release because both of its data targets (DA-PAY, DA-TCK) are blocked by open critical verification obligations (VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE, VOB-U-RESPONSE-TIME-METRIC-SCOPE).
domain_authorizations is currently empty and the tool surface (ticket-db, payment-db) is read-only, so none of the released actions can actually execute until a human grants write authorization.

Whether IBAN-format failures represent a material share of the overall ticket backlog (versus other causes like self-service visibility gaps or process delay) remains open (U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION-SHARE, U-COMPETING-MECHANISMS) and was not resolved before release.
Preventive IBAN validation at refund intake (process change to P-REF) was identified as a root-cause fix but left unfinished/out of release scope.
